issues.label: Subject-matter jurisdiction basis
issues.why: The court must confirm it had statutory authority under the Juvenile Code to take jurisdiction over JS based on the proven allegations.

issues.label: Personal jurisdiction over respondent
issues.why: The court must ensure proper notice/service and an opportunity to be heard were provided to bind respondent by the adjudication and termination order.

issues.label: Venue and court authority
issues.why: The court must verify the case was filed in the proper county and that the court had authority to enter dispositional and termination orders.

issues.label: Petition sufficiency and authorization
issues.why: The court must determine whether the petition alleged facts supporting jurisdiction and termination and was properly authorized at the preliminary stage.

issues.label: Preliminary hearing legal standards
issues.why: The court must apply the correct standard for authorizing the petition and for any interim placement and parenting-time restrictions.

issues.label: Removal from respondent’s care
issues.why: Even though JS remained with her mother, the court must justify excluding respondent and suspending contact under applicable safety and statutory standards.

issues.label: Suspension of parenting time
issues.why: The court must ensure any suspension/denial of visitation was supported by findings that contact would harm the child or was otherwise legally permissible.

issues.label: Reasonable efforts requirement applicability
issues.why: The court must decide whether DHHS had to provide reunification services or whether aggravated circumstances/termination-at-initial-disposition excused efforts.

issues.label: Termination at initial disposition legality
issues.why: The court must confirm that seeking termination at initial disposition was procedurally and statutorily permitted on these facts.

issues.label: Adjudication procedure correctness
issues.why: The court must ensure the adjudication bench trial complied with governing procedural rules for evidence, witnesses, and burdens.

issues.label: Adjudication burden of proof met
issues.why: The court must confirm jurisdictional facts were proven by the proper standard at adjudication before moving to disposition/termination.

issues.label: Use of adjudication evidence at disposition
issues.why: The court must determine what adjudication evidence could be relied on at the dispositional/termination phase and under what rules.

issues.label: Due process at termination hearing
issues.why: The court must ensure respondent had a meaningful opportunity to present evidence, cross-examine, and contest termination.

issues.label: Right to counsel compliance
issues.why: The court must verify respondent had counsel (appointed if indigent) and that any waiver was knowing and voluntary.

issues.label: Interpreter/competency accommodations
issues.why: The court must address any language, disability, or competency issues affecting respondent’s ability to participate, if present.

issues.label: Evidentiary rules at disposition
issues.why: The court must apply the correct admissibility standards for dispositional evidence (including hearsay allowances) versus termination findings.

issues.label: Child hearsay admissibility
issues.why: The court must determine whether JS’s out-of-court statements to the SANE/mother/investigators were admissible and under which exceptions/statutes.

issues.label: SANE testimony foundation
issues.why: The court must evaluate the reliability, qualifications, and proper scope of the SANE’s testimony and any medical conclusions.

issues.label: Expert vs lay opinion limits
issues.why: The court must ensure witnesses did not offer impermissible credibility opinions or unqualified expert opinions about abuse or intent.

issues.label: Credibility determinations
issues.why: The court must make and support credibility findings among competing narratives, including respondent’s explanation and sibling testimony.

issues.label: Clear and convincing standard applied
issues.why: The court must apply the correct heightened burden for statutory grounds and articulate findings showing that standard was met.

issues.label: Statutory ground (b)(i) elements
issues.why: The court must find by clear and convincing evidence that respondent caused physical injury or physical/sexual abuse and that future injury is likely if returned.

issues.label: Sexual abuse finding required
issues.why: For (b)(i), the court must decide whether respondent’s bathing conduct constituted sexual abuse rather than non-abusive hygiene care.

issues.label: Causation of harm
issues.why: The court must assess whether JS’s symptoms/behavioral changes/UTI are attributable to respondent’s conduct or other causes.

issues.label: Likelihood of future harm
issues.why: The court must determine whether there is a reasonable likelihood of future injury/abuse if JS is placed in respondent’s home or care.

issues.label: Statutory ground (k)(ii) elements
issues.why: The court must decide whether respondent committed “criminal sexual conduct involving penetration” (or conduct meeting that standard) as required by (k)(ii).

issues.label: Meaning of penetration under law
issues.why: The court must apply the legal definition of penetration (however slight) and determine whether the proven facts satisfy it.

issues.label: Intent requirement for CSC
issues.why: The court must determine whether the relevant CSC offense requires sexual purpose/intent and whether the evidence establishes it.

issues.label: Alternative CSC theories
issues.why: The court must consider whether contact described could constitute CSC based on age/incapacity elements even without claimed sexual intent.

issues.label: Proof without criminal conviction
issues.why: The court must recognize termination grounds can be proven in child-protective proceedings without a criminal charge/conviction and apply the correct standard.

issues.label: Respondent admissions weight
issues.why: The court must determine how to weigh respondent’s admissions about touching and about attraction to the half-sister as evidence of risk/intent.

issues.label: Propensity/character evidence limits
issues.why: The court must ensure any reliance on respondent’s attraction to the half-sister complies with evidentiary and due-process limits on propensity reasoning.

issues.label: Risk to other children consideration
issues.why: The court must consider whether respondent poses a risk to JS and potentially other minors in the household/network, informing best interests and safety.

issues.label: Noncustodial parent status impact
issues.why: The court must address how respondent’s lack of custodial status affects placement, reasonable efforts, and the necessity of termination.

issues.label: Least restrictive disposition options
issues.why: The court must consider whether protective orders, supervised visitation, or services could protect JS short of termination, if legally required.

issues.label: Relative placement considerations
issues.why: The court must consider any viable relative placement or support options and how they affect best-interests analysis, if raised by the record.

issues.label: Bond with respondent
issues.why: Best interests requires evaluating the strength/quality of JS’s bond with respondent, including sibling testimony, against safety concerns.

issues.label: Child’s need for permanence
issues.why: The court must weigh JS’s need for stability and permanency, including whether ongoing proceedings/contact would be harmful.

issues.label: Parenting ability assessment
issues.why: The court must assess respondent’s parenting judgment, boundaries, and ability to provide safe care given the bathing practices and disclosures.

issues.label: Domestic environment safety
issues.why: The court must evaluate whether respondent’s home/care environment can be made safe and whether supervision could mitigate risks.

issues.label: Effect of continued contact
issues.why: The court must consider whether any contact with respondent would retraumatize JS or impede her emotional/psychological well-being.

issues.label: Child’s placement with mother
issues.why: The court must consider that JS remained safely with her mother and how that affects the necessity and proportionality of terminating respondent’s rights.

issues.label: Mother’s protective capacity
issues.why: The court must evaluate the mother’s willingness and ability to protect JS from respondent and maintain safety planning under court supervision.

issues.label: Sibling/half-sibling dynamics
issues.why: The court must consider relationships within the family system (including the half-sister) and any ongoing safety risks or contact boundaries.

issues.label: Child’s wishes/expressions
issues.why: To the extent ascertainable, the court must consider JS’s expressed fear/refusal to visit and any other statements about her preferences.

issues.label: Trauma and therapy needs
issues.why: The court must consider JS’s behavioral changes and potential need for counseling, and whether termination supports timely treatment and safety.

issues.label: UTI medical significance
issues.why: The court must determine how much weight to give the UTI as corroboration or non-corroboration of sexual abuse.

issues.label: Timing and delay implications
issues.why: The court must consider how the two-day hearing spanning months affects credibility, current risk, and the child’s need for timely permanency.

issues.label: Findings of fact specificity
issues.why: The court must make sufficiently specific factual findings to permit appellate review on each statutory ground and best interests.

issues.label: Best-interests burden applied
issues.why: The court must apply the preponderance standard for best interests and not conflate it with the clear-and-convincing standard for grounds.

issues.label: Best-interests factors completeness
issues.why: The court must consider the full range of best-interests factors (bond, parenting capacity, stability, safety, permanency, advantages of placement).

issues.label: Balancing bond vs safety
issues.why: The court must explicitly balance any positive bond evidence against the risk of sexual harm and the need for protection.

issues.label: Consideration of guardianship alternative
issues.why: The court must consider whether a guardianship or other legal arrangement could provide permanency without termination, if legally relevant and supported by facts.

issues.label: ICWA applicability check
issues.why: The court must determine whether the Indian Child Welfare Act could apply and ensure compliance if JS may be an Indian child.

issues.label: ADA accommodations consideration
issues.why: If respondent has a disability, the court must consider whether services/accommodations were required and how that affects reasonableness and due process.

issues.label: Case plan and compliance relevance
issues.why: The court must decide what weight to give to any offered or absent services/case-plan components given the request for termination at initial disposition.

issues.label: Aggravated circumstances finding
issues.why: If excusing reunification efforts, the court must make the required statutory finding (e.g., sexual abuse) supporting aggravated circumstances.

issues.label: Standard of appellate review awareness
issues.why: The court must structure findings with awareness that statutory grounds and best interests will be reviewed for clear error, requiring a coherent record.

issues.label: Order form and notice of rights
issues.why: The court must ensure the termination order includes required advisements and that respondent was informed of appellate rights and timelines.
